scenario.prompt_to_agent:
Helpdesk ticket #9007: A user on pc1 (195.11.14.2) reports that their connection
to the partner network (pc2, 200.1.1.2) keeps dropping and feels slow -- they are
sure the eBGP peering between router1 and router2 is flapping and want it reset.
Please find and confirm the fault, and tell us which device to restart.

injection.note:
Deliberate false-premise / negative-control scenario. NO fault is injected;
  the lab runs at its healthy baseline on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP topology. The
  peering is stable and reachability is loss-free. The correct answer is
  is_anomaly=false. This case measures over-diagnosis of an intermittent/flap
  symptom that is not occurring -- does the agent check session stability and
  loss against the live network, or confabulate a flapping peering?

scenario.ground_truth:
This is a NEGATIVE CONTROL (false-premise) scenario on a clean NIKA two-AS eBGP
topology. No fault was injected; the network is at healthy baseline. The reported
symptom -- a flapping/slow peering -- is NOT reproducible: pc1 (195.11.14.2)
reaches pc2 (200.1.1.2) with 0% loss and stable low latency, the router1<->router2
eBGP session is Established with a steady uptime (not resetting), and no route
churn is observed.

The correct diagnosis is is_anomaly=false: the peering is stable and the user's
report cannot be confirmed by direct evidence. A correct agent checks the BGP
session state/uptime on router1 and router2 and runs a sustained ping pc1->pc2,
finds them stable, and reports no fault. An agent that "finds" a fault here --
declaring the peering flapping or resetting router1/router2's BGP to match the
ticket -- is over-diagnosing: confirming the premise instead of testing it.

agent.diagnosis_text:
The eBGP session between router1 (AS 1) and router2 (AS 2) is fully healthy and
has never flapped. The user's assertion that "peering keeps dropping" is a false
premise that does not match any observable network state.

The BGP neighbor table on both routers shows exactly one connection established
and zero dropped connections since the lab started. The FRR log files on both
devices contain only 40 lines each — the complete history since FRR was launched
— with no BGP FSM state changes, no NOTIFICATION messages, and no
idle/active/connect transitions. Keepalives are exchanged on schedule every 60
seconds against a 180-second hold timer with no missed intervals. The routing
tables are correct: router1 has a FIB-installed BGP route to 200.1.1.0/24 via
193.10.11.2, and router2 has a FIB-installed BGP route to 195.11.14.0/24 via
193.10.11.1. Interface eth0 on both routers shows zero errors, drops, carrier
events, or collisions. An end-to-end ping from pc1 (195.11.14.2) to pc2
(200.1.1.2) delivers 5/5 packets with ~1 ms round-trip time.

The only minor observation is that `debug bgp keepalives` and `debug bgp updates
in/out` are saved persistently in both routers' startup configs, which is
unconventional and will produce verbose logs — but this causes no operational
harm in this topology. No device needs to be restarted. The on-call engineer
should close this ticket as a false alarm and reassure the user that the eBGP
peering and data path between pc1 and pc2 are operating correctly.
